Built a physical simulation of a record player with WebGL2 and Web Audio. It's *shockingly* accurate: https://t.co/MBNaTfKoai.

Instead of playing a song, it works by converting it into the physical shape of a groove. Then a simulated stylus rides those walls 384,000 times a second, and you hear the voltage that motion would induce in a cartridge.

So the crackle, the pops, the wow/flutter, the dull inner grooves are natural byproducts of the simulation. You can also "DJ" the record.

(The converted songs are in the public domain or CC-licensed. Code is linked for you to remix and re-deploy.)

tweets.text:
We’re moving from an era of AI where the output comes roughly at the rate that you can chat back and forth with the AI to work with you, to a period where you can set a problem for a set of agents to go off and do an arbitrarily large amount of work for you. This means productivity gains that are maybe 20-50% to gains that don’t really have an upper limit.

Agent swarms and the ability to fan out complex work across many agents doing tasks in parallel provide a massive unlock in a lot of spaces. This will lead to qualitatively different outcomes in my fields. 

This has already been seen across the coding domain. Next, cyber is almost entirely a problem space where more agents reviewing more things will lead to far better outcomes. We’re seeing the same now in many scientific fields, and this almost certainly will change life sciences. 

But this will increasingly be true in any field where you can parallelize computer-based work to complete something faster or do something at a totally different quality level. Which is actually are some of the most valuable domains of knowledge work today. 

Our brains aren’t really wired for the new scenario we’re heading into where compute becomes the variable that we can flex to solve any problem that we want. We’re used to thinking that the amount of time that goes into a task is correlated to the output that we get from it. And most domains of knowledge work or science have generally always been correlated with this. That’s changing forever.

A good lesson in AI is that you need to check back in on the latest with every 3 to 6 months to try something that wasn’t possible before and see if it works again.

At no point in AI’s history is that more true than today. Just the past six months of model progress around computer and tool use, less context rot, better reasoning, multimodality, and deeper domain expertise in a number of key fields, these models are vastly more capable on what they can execute.

This is opening up a new vector of what AI systems will be able to autonomously work on. Essentially, anything with an API (and even many things without), we can anticipate that an agent will be able to control and utilize as an underlying capability to complete a process.

This means that we are no longer dependent on *just* the models generating everything from whole cloth, but instead they can fully utilize existing systems (or new ones purpose built for them) very effectively. This creates immense leverage for agents.

Security agents can leverage existing data feeds and cyber tooling, IT agents that can execute workflows reliably across software stacks, data agents that can migrate data or processes between systems, architect and design agents can leverage CAD and design tools, and on and on. And any of today’s tools that don’t work will likely be replaced by agent-friendly or OSS tooling that does the same. 

When you combine this with the domain understanding being trained into agents, you started to get autonomous collaborators for every job function and industry. This will open up a ton of new opportunities in AI if you build with this understanding in mind.

If you are visiting SF, and trying to meet more people, here are a random list of things you should remove from your vocabulary..

> swap notes
> "synergies"
> pick your brain
> networking
> "san fran" (tourist tell)
> grab coffee if you're free

If you want to meet interesting people here, show your work. The most interesting people I know in the city are not attending that fancy large conference - they are probably at their office. 

So what's the work? It can be as simple as a thoughtful cold email, a five line pointed DM, or complex as some side projects that you have shipped, or a meetup that you are organizing.

If you put in the effort, it shows, yes, even in this AI era. I still get so much slop across the board, that if I see anyone put in the effort, I try to go out of my way to meet them. 

Even the busiest people have 15 mins to give you, if you give them a reason to!

The guest is Mihail Eric, who is not only teaching the Modern Software Developer at Stanford, which is going viral right now for basically covering all the AI-native development pract- best practices, uh, but also he is head of AI at Monaco.

So he's not only a teacher, but he's a practitioner. Um, and those of you coming to AIU Code Summit next week, um, it's gonna be the celebration of all the extreme progress that you've seen in coding in the last year.

I'm excited about all the themes of fighting slop, of system one models, and of increasing your ambition for major rewrites of basically everything that you've seen in code.

Um, there's never been a more exciting time to be an AI engineer, and with one million AI engineers, I think it's just getting started. So let's get into the interview.

Okay, we're in the studio with Mihail Eric, Adjunct Professor at Stanford and Head of AI at Monaco. Welcome. Thank you. I'm glad to be here.

You caught our attention because of your course that you are refreshing for the third time, third year? Second time. Second time? Yep. The CS 146, or 146S, the Modern Software Developer at Stanford.

This particular generation of junior developers, of junior engineers, the people that are now entering the workforce, will, I think, be the first kind of generation of that new shift.

And I looked at the syllabus, and I was like, "This is everything we cover." So every now and then, I like to invite people like yourself who, like, you cover a broad range of topics- Mm-hmm...

and then we can sort of go topic by topic and give people the state of the art- Yeah... on each of these things, which I, I assume you're doing with all your guests anyway. For sure. Tell us the history of the course.

What made you wanna spring out CS 146? Yeah. So this is the second time it's being taught, and I taught it for the first time last fall, so fall 2025. This was pre, like, Opus 4.5, 4.6 days.

But the-- Even before fall 2025, the course had been about, like, a year in the making.

The genesis of the class was like November of 2024, and I had sort of had this idea that we're seeing all this stuff happening in coding agents, and yes, they were an earlier version of the coding agents, but already it felt like there was something drastically changing in terms of how developers were doing their work, how quickly we were getting work done, uh, all that fun stuff.

And so at the time, I just-- It was all just scattered blog posts, scattered, like, things you could find online if you were trying to really get into the, the methodology of how to do these things.

And so I, I had this idea like, "Hey, well, is there a way to kind of structure a curriculum around this that's a little bit more formal?" Had the idea.

And you know, I, my alma mater is Stanford, and I always had this dream to go back and teach something and, and kind of pay it forward. Uh, I've always been very deep into education.

I talked to Chip, who also taught a class, uh, one of my good friends. Chip Hieatt. Yeah. Yeah, Chip Hieatt, exactly. Uh, spoke to her.

Who-- She had taught her, I guess, designing machine learning systems, and so, like, asked her what that process was like, and sort of, you know, took a lot of inspiration for how she-- from how she designed the curriculum and, and thought about, you know, getting something through the, through the school.

Put it together, spent about nine to ten months. This was now fall of 2024 through to, like, you know, mid to late of 2025. Got it through the committee, uh, made a case for the class to exist.

You know, I had to put together a proposal and everything. Uh, and that took me to fall 2025, when I taught it for the first time, which was very well-received. You know, students were really interested in it.

Uh, there was even, I guess, like, a Business Insider article that was written about the class last year. And then, yeah, this year, uh, a lot of things changed.

I would say really coding agents, autonomous coding agents really have picked up- [laughs]... in a way that, that we had not seen before.

Um, so it felt like it was time to do this again, uh, refresh things, uh, and here we are. M-Meanwhile, you're also head of AI at Monaco- Yeah... which is also a very buzzy startup. Yes, yes.

We are, we are, we are, we're in the airwaves right now and, and, uh, having a fun time doing it. Yeah. Yeah. Uh, so, like, I, I do like that you're also, I guess, a practitioner.

You guys are obviously implementing all this stuff at Monaco. Yeah. Any, I guess, principles or observations about just what you have changed from last year to this year at a high level? Yeah, yeah. I mean, a ton.

I think that

when I reflect on what last year's version of the class was, uh, I mean, coding agents had been around, but we were still in kind of that phase where companies were emerging that were tackling every single part of, like, the ISDLC.

There was, like, a coding agent for code review. There was a coding agent for, you know, spec design. There was a coding agent for, uh, SRE. And, you know, some of those-- Of course, some of those companies still exist.

But it felt like last year it was a lot more about a broad tour of here's everywhere you can use coding agents.

And in a way, a lot of the curriculum last year was, was geared toward exposure and this, this kind of survey, this kind of like odyssey of sorts through, hey, everything that you knew a-about the ISDLC is now changing because of AI.

Um, this year I think there's some principles that are solidifying, right? The idea of, like, very careful context engineering.

The idea of, like, really thinking through sort of like design and architecture as a way of handling really complex tasks. And so the nature of my class is it's not intended for the, like, beginner programmer.

It is not a, it is not a replacement for, like, traditional computer science in the sense of, like, algorithms and if-- In fact, a lot of those classes are prereqs to what I'm, what I'm doing here.

But I do know that you-- if you have a good foundation, going now toward applying that and, and, and sort of using those principles in, in production environments in, like, real world, that's something that I think is, is now at a place where...
